jurisdictions.title: Virginia noxious weeds (2VAC5-317) and invasive plant signage law (Code of Virginia § 3.2-3801.1)
jurisdictions.edition: Virginia Administrative Code, 2VAC5-317 as last amended effective July 4, 2024 (Virginia Register Vol. 40, Iss. 21); Code of Virginia §§ 3.2-800 to 3.2-809 as amended through 2026, and § 3.2-3801.1 (2025, cc. 393, 409), effective January 1, 2027; both as printed by the General Assembly's Legislative Information System on 2026-10-31

classes.tier1: Noxious weed in Virginia: a Tier 1 weed, not known to be present in the state; it may not be moved (shipped, carried or otherwise transported) without a certificate or permit from the Commissioner, who may destroy or seize it, or stop its sale or delivery (2VAC5-317-20, -30, -80)
classes.tier2: Noxious weed in Virginia: a Tier 2 weed, present in the state and feasible to eradicate or suppress; it may not be moved (shipped, carried or otherwise transported) without a certificate or permit from the Commissioner, who may destroy or seize it, or stop its sale or delivery (2VAC5-317-20, -30, -80)
classes.tier3: Noxious weed in Virginia: a Tier 3 weed, present in the state and not feasible to eradicate or suppress; it may not be moved (shipped, carried or otherwise transported) without a certificate or permit from the Commissioner (2VAC5-317-20, -30)
classes.invasive: Invasive plant in Virginia: from January 1, 2027, a store may sell it for outdoor use only with a sign near it that identifies it as invasive; the Commissioner must stop the sale of any without one (Code of Virginia § 3.2-3801.1)

jurisdictions.notes: The rule prints "Oplismenus hirtellus spp. undulatifolius" (wavyleaf basketgrass): "spp." is read as subspecies and written "subsp.", since the list format has no place for the misprinted rank. All three tiers carry the same duty: "The movement of a regulated article is prohibited unless accompanied by a valid certificate or permit" (2VAC5-317-30), where "move" means to ship, offer for shipment, receive for transportation, carry, or otherwise transport, move, or allow to be moved. The rule says nothing of selling, planting or propagating as such; the statute requires a permit before selling or offering for sale a noxious weed into or within the state where the Board requires one (§ 3.2-804), and the Board's rule requires one for movement. Tiered as bans because moving the plant within the state is forbidden without a permit; permits are for movement to a specified destination under limited handling, use, processing or treatment, or for experimental or scientific purposes (2VAC5-317-40). Tiers 1 and 2 differ from Tier 3 only in that the Commissioner may eradicate or suppress them, by destruction, seizure, stop sale, stop delivery, treatment or return to origin (2VAC5-317-80). The statute's definition of "move" (§ 3.2-800) excepts "bona fide agricultural purposes including the management, tilling, planting, or harvesting of agricultural products"; the rule's own definition doesn't repeat the exception. Phase-out: § 3.2-802 A, updated in 2026 (2026, c. 66), gives any plant commercially propagated in Virginia a phase-out "upon being designated as a noxious weed" of two years for grasses, forbs and vines, four for shrubs and seven for trees. The rule names no plant as being phased out, and the statute doesn't say whether this reaches plants listed before 2026. The 2024 additions (Trapa bispinosa to Tier 2; Alliaria petiolata through Ulmus pumila to Tier 3, effective July 4, 2024) were proposed when the statute's definition of noxious weed still excluded plants commercially propagated in Virginia (quoted in the Virginia Register, Vol. 40, Iss. 2, 2023). Phragmites australis and Pueraria montana are listed as species, with no subspecies or variety excepted. The invasive class (§ 3.2-3801.1) takes effect January 1, 2027, and until then has no force. It is tiered listed: selling stays legal with the signs, which must identify the plant as invasive, educate consumers about invasive plant species and encourage them to ask about alternatives; without them the Commissioner must issue a stop-sale order until the signs are posted. It names botanical names only. Kew's accepted names, checked in its checklist (2026-10-31): Egeria densa, Ficaria verna, Mahonia bealei, Oshuna crassipes and Securigera varia are homotypic synonyms of Elodea densa, Ranunculus ficaria, Berberis bealei, Pontederia crassipes (water hyacinth) and Coronilla varia; Cenchrus purpurascens Thunb. is a heterotypic synonym of Cenchrus alopecuroides (Chinese fountain grass, sold as Pennisetum alopecuroides), and is matched as that species. Kew makes Trapa bispinosa a variety of Trapa natans, and Ampelopsis brevipedunculata a variety of Ampelopsis glandulosa, so both are matched by their printed names only (a listed species would take in the whole species, and the other varieties are not listed). Left out: the Department of Conservation and Recreation's invasive plant list (§ 10.1-104.6:2), which the law has DCR create and which binds only state agencies (no agency may plant, sell or propagate its plants), the list itself not being printed in law; and the tradesperson-notice rule § 3.2-802 C calls for, proposed as 2VAC5-455 in February 2025 and not in the Administrative Code as of 2026-10-31. Also left out: the box tree moth quarantine (2VAC5-332, effective March 11, 2026), which needs a certificate or permit to move Buxus from Clarke and Frederick Counties and the City of Winchester to unregulated areas, a pest quarantine on a host plant in named places, not statewide; and, not read, the seed law (2VAC5-390) and the endangered plant rule (2VAC5-320), which protects plants rather than restricting them.

jurisdictions.title: Georgia live plant rules: federal noxious weeds (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 40-4-9-.07)
jurisdictions.edition: Rules of the Georgia Department of Agriculture, Rules 40-4-9-.07 and 40-4-9-.11 as amended effective October 13, 2010, in the Secretary of State's compilation current through rules filed through October 22, 2026; the plants are 7 CFR 360.200's, Code of Federal Regulations revised as of January 1, 2025

classes.federal: Federal noxious weed in Georgia: its sale or distribution in the state is prohibited (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 40-4-9-.07)

jurisdictions.notes: The rule names no plant of its own. It prohibits "The sale or distribution of any plant listed on the Federal Noxious Weed list or determined by the Commissioner to be a public nuisance" (40-4-9-.07(1); also an unlawful act, 40-4-9-.11(b)), and a Federal Noxious Weed is "Any plant listed under Title 7, Code of Federal Regulations, Part 360" (40-4-9-.01(h)). So this list adopts the US entry's plants (7 CFR 360.200), by reference, as the rule does: it names no edition, so it changes whenever the federal list does. No plant "determined by the Commissioner to be a public nuisance" was found: the rules name none, and their former subject "Declaration of Public Nuisance" (40-4-22) was repealed effective October 16, 2013. The rule forbids sale and distribution; it says nothing of a plant already growing on someone's land. Out-of-state growers and dealers may sell live plants into Georgia only if they "are not designated as a Federal Noxious Weed" (40-4-9-.04(1)(a)). Breaking the chapter is a misdemeanor (40-4-9-.12(4)). The Secretary of State's robots.txt closes the single-rule pages to crawlers; the text was read from the subject page and the history from the Department 40 PDF, both on the same official site and both allowed. Left out: the seed rule (40-12-4-.01), with its own noxious weed seed list; and the pest and disease quarantines, which certify host plants rather than restrict them as weeds: vegetable transplants entering Georgia (40-4-7), phony peach (40-4-13), blueberry scorch virus (Vaccinium, 40-4-24) and citrus (Citrus and related genera, and Murraya, 40-4-26). Not read: the statute (O.C.G.A. Title 2, Chapter 7), whose official online text is published through LexisNexis's web application; the rule cites O.C.G.A. §§ 2-7-1 et seq. and 2-7-14 as its authority and sets the effect itself.

classes.classBPrivet: Class B noxious weed in Pennsylvania: it may not be sold, offered for sale, given away, imported, transported, cultivated or propagated in the state, except under an individual permit for research or education; the Department of Agriculture exempts the cultivar 'Golden Ticket' (3 Pa.C.S. §§1502, 1515(b), 1519(b); the Department's exempted varieties)

jurisdictions.notes: The statute lists the first noxious weeds (§1519); the Controlled Plant and Noxious Weed Committee adds plants by notice in the Pennsylvania Bulletin, effective 60 days after publication (§1511(b)(3)(iv)). The full lists are read from the Department of Agriculture's list page: the Bulletin notices, and any sales phase-in they set, could not be read, as pacodeandbulletin.gov's robots.txt shuts out all but named crawlers. Neither saved department page gives a phase-in date. Every plant §1519 names is on the department's page. Hydrilla verticillata, Class A in §1519(a), is Class B on the department's page, and is shown as B (same effect). Wavyleaf basketgrass: the department prints Oplismenus hirtellus; it is recorded narrower, as the statute prints it, "Oplismenus hirtellus (L.) P. Beauv. Subsp. undulatifolius" (§1519(a)(9)). Japanese blood grass: the department lists "Imperata cylindrica 'Red Baron'" in Class A, a cultivar the list format can't name; it isn't recorded there, since the whole species is on the federal list, which makes it a Class C noxious weed here, under the same ban. Class C is every federal noxious weed not established in Pennsylvania and not otherwise listed (§1519(c)); §1502 makes every federal noxious weed a noxious weed here. So this list adopts the US entry's plants into Class C, by reference (the department's page: "includes the Federal Noxious Weed list by default as Class C weeds"); Stratiotes aloides, which the department names, is recorded as well. A plant on both lists takes its Pennsylvania class first. Left out: "Cuscuta spp., except for native species" and "Orobanche spp., except for native species", since the rule names neither the natives it spares nor the others (the federally listed dodders and broomrapes are in the US entry); Nitellopsis obtusa (starry stonewort), an alga; "Sorghum bicolor L. Moench (commonly known as shattercane)", which names no weedy form and read whole would make grain sorghum a noxious weed; "Pastinaca sativa (except for non-wild cultivated varieties)", wild parsnip, which a species name can't tell from the garden parsnip the rule excepts. Lythrum: "Exotic Lythrum species, including Lythrum salicaria L. (commonly known as purple loosestrife), the Lythrum salicaria complex and Lythrum virgatum L. (commonly known as European wand loosestrife), their cultivars and any combination thereof": the two named species are recorded. Amaranthus rudis and A. tuberculatus are printed as two entries. Printed with synonyms, recorded by the first name: Tripidium ravennae [Saccharum ravennae, Erianthus ravennae]; Cynanchum louiseae/Vincetoxicum nigrum; Cynanchum rossicum/Vincetoxicum rossicum; Rhamnus frangula [Frangula alnus]; Persicaria perfoliata ("formerly known as Polygonum perfoliatum L."). Exempted cultivars, on the department's exempted-varieties page (https://www.pa.gov/en/agencies/pda/plants-land-water/plant-industry/noxious-weeds-and-controlled-plants/exempted-varieties-information-application.html, read 2026-10-31), named in the line for each of the three species, since the list format names no cultivar: Japanese barberry, the WorryFree series Crimson Cutie (UCONNBTCP4N), Lemon Cutie (UCONNBTB113), Lemon Glow (UCONNBTB048) and Mr. Green Genes (UCONNBTB039), and Proven Winners Sunjoy Todo and Sunjoy Mini-Maroon; glossy buckthorn, Rhamnus 'Fine Line'; European privet, 'Golden Ticket'. The statute itself has no section on exempting cultivars. Permits: a noxious weed may be cultivated and propagated only under an individual permit for research and educational purposes (§1512(a)(1)); controlled plants under a general or individual permit (§§1512 to 1514). Hemp is listed as a controlled plant on the department's page; the committee's notice and Pennsylvania's hemp chapter were not read. Not read: 7 Pa. Code Ch. 110 (pacodeandbulletin.gov's robots.txt); the law it was made under, the Noxious Weed Control Law of 1982, was repealed by Act 46 of 2017, §3(2). Seed law (7 Pa. Code Ch. 111, which §1511(c) points weed seeds to) is left out. Kew's accepted names, checked in its checklist (2026-10-31): Cynanchum louiseae, Cynanchum rossicum, Egeria densa, Ficaria verna and Rhamnus frangula are homotypic synonyms of Vincetoxicum nigrum, Vincetoxicum rossicum, Elodea densa, Ranunculus ficaria and Frangula alnus; Amaranthus rudis and Humulus japonicus are heterotypic synonyms of Amaranthus tuberculatus and Humulus scandens (Japanese hops), and are matched as those species. Kew makes Pueraria lobata a variety (Pueraria montana var. lobata) and Lonicera standishii part of Lonicera fragrantissima subsp. fragrantissima, so both are matched by their printed names only.

jurisdictions.title: Kentucky noxious weeds and invasive plants on state rights-of-way (KRS 176.051; 603 KAR 3:100)
jurisdictions.edition: 603 KAR 3:100 effective January 25, 2022 (48 Ky.R. 1434, 2075); KRS 176.051 as amended 2017, effective June 29, 2017 (Kentucky Legislative Research Commission)

classes.rightofway: Noxious weed or invasive plant under Kentucky law: the state Department of Highways must keep state rights-of-way free of it (KRS 176.051; 603 KAR 3:100)

jurisdictions.notes: No Kentucky law found bans selling or planting a named plant. The one plant list beyond seed law is KRS 176.051(1), as 603 KAR 3:100 amends it: it binds the Department of Highways on state rights-of-way (and its help to abutting owners who ask), not landowners, nurseries or gardeners. Only three entries print a botanical name: Sorghum halepense, Cirsium arvense and Carduus nutans. Left out, common names only: multiflora rose, kudzu, poison hemlock, marestail, Amur honeysuckle, Japanese knotweed and common teasel (KRS 176.051(1)), and spotted knapweed and cutleaf teasel (added by 603 KAR 3:100, Section 1(1)); "marestail" could mean more than one plant. Giant foxtail, a common name only, was deleted by 603 KAR 3:100, Section 1(2). Checked and left out: the seed law's noxious weed seed list (12 KAR 1:120, limits on weed seed in agricultural seed); KRS Chapter 249, whose thistle laws (KRS 249.180 to 249.195: landholders to cut Canada thistles, thistle eradication areas) were repealed by 2022 Ky. Acts ch. 131, effective July 14, 2022, and whose remaining noxious weed sections (KRS 249.420, 249.430) let the Department of Agriculture run control programs and issue regulations but name no plant; 302 KAR (Department of Agriculture), which has no noxious weed or invasive plant regulation; KRS 249.040 quarantines, which are against plants carrying insect pests or plant diseases and name no plant; 301 KAR 1:122 (Fish and Wildlife), which bars buying, selling or releasing "any aquatic species not native or established in Kentucky waters" (aquarium use excepted) but names only animals, so gives no plant list. 2025 House Bill 640, to let the Energy and Environment Cabinet regulate invasive non-native plants, did not pass (last action March 12, 2025: to the Senate's Committee on Committees).

classes.aquatic: Noxious aquatic weed in North Carolina: the state may control, remove or destroy it in the state's waters or where it threatens to invade them (15A NCAC 02G .0602; G.S. 113A-223)

jurisdictions.notes: The Administrative Code itself (the Office of Administrative Hearings' site, reports.oah.state.nc.us) could not be read: it is served only over http, and its https port does not answer from here. So 02 NCAC 48A .1702 and .1703 are read in the North Carolina Register's printing of the rules as approved (26:09, November 1, 2011). OAH's periodic review report for 02 NCAC 48A (submitted January 22, 2019) still gives October 1, 2011 as the last amendment of both rules, and the Department of Agriculture's current noxious weed list names the same plants; an amendment after 2019 could not be ruled out without the Code. Not read, for the same reason: .1701 (definitions), .1704 (regulated articles), .1705 and .1706 (the certificates and limited permits that are the rule's only exception), .1707 and .1708. Class A item (1) is "All weeds listed in 7 C.F.R. 360.200 which is hereby incorporated by reference including subsequent amendments and editions": so this list adopts the US entry's plants into Class A, by reference; its own entries come first. "Salvinia spp. (all except S. minima)" is the genus, with Salvinia minima excepted (the rule abbreviates the genus). The rule prints "Trappa spp." (water-chestnut): entered as the genus Trapa, which the Environmental Quality rule prints, since a genus entry carries no Kew spelling. Read narrower than printed: Class B's "Lythrum – Any Lythrum species not native to North Carolina", which names no species, as purple loosestrife, Lythrum salicaria, which 15A NCAC 02G .0602 names and the Department of Agriculture's list calls this entry ("Purple loosestrife (Lythrum spp. not native to NC)"); other non-native Lythrum are covered by the rule but not entered, because a genus entry would take in North Carolina's native Lythrum species, which the rule excepts without naming them. Class C: "regulated area" is read as the counties .1703(a)(14) names for Oriental bittersweet (the rule's heading is "Regulated Areas"; .1701, which may define it, was not read); inside those counties the rule does not forbid selling it, but forbids moving it out; tiered ban because it forbids moving it into the state. Class B and C plants each have named counties they may not be moved from (.1703(a)(1)-(3), (6)-(14)). Violating these rules is a Class 3 misdemeanor (G.S. 106-423.1). Noxious aquatic weeds: the Department of Environmental Quality designates them (G.S. 113A-222); the statute lets the Secretary control them in the state's waters (G.S. 113A-223) and lets the Commissioner of Agriculture regulate their sale as plant pests under the plant pest law (G.S. 113A-224), and neither the statute nor .0602 forbids selling or growing them, so tiered listed; the section's other rule, 15A NCAC 02G .0601, was not read. Left out of the aquatic class: the 16 species printed under "Species Listed on the Federal Noxious Weed List" that are still on it (shown by the federal entry, and Class A by .1702(a)(1)); and Crassula helmsii, Lagarosiphon spp., Ludwigia hexapetala, Lythrum salicaria, Myriophyllum spicatum, Salvinia spp. ("All except S. rotundifolia") and Trapa spp., which are on 02 NCAC 48A and shown there. Stratiotes aloides is printed under the federal heading but is no longer a federal noxious weed: entered here. Phragmites australis is printed as the whole species, the native American subspecies too. The Environmental Quality copy of .0602 names the Department of Environment and Natural Resources and may differ from the codified text. Not included: the seed rules (02 NCAC 48C), the witchweed quarantine (02 NCAC 48A .0500, not read; Striga is on the federal list), and advisory lists. Kew's accepted names, checked in its checklist (2026-10-31): Cayratia japonica, Egeria densa and Eichhornia crassipes are homotypic synonyms of Causonis japonica, Elodea densa and Pontederia crassipes; Nymphoides cristata is a heterotypic synonym of Nymphoides hydrophyllum, and is matched as that species.

jurisdictions.title: Ohio invasive plants (OAC 901:5-30-01) and prohibited noxious weeds (OAC 901:5-37-01)
jurisdictions.edition: Ohio Administrative Code 901:5-30-01 effective February 13, 2023 and 901:5-37-01 effective February 16, 2025; Ohio Revised Code 927.682 effective July 9, 1986, 5579.04 effective June 11, 1991 and 5579.05 effective April 3, 2025, as published on codes.ohio.gov

classes.invasive: Invasive plant in Ohio: no one may sell, offer for sale, propagate, distribute, import or intentionally cause the dissemination of it in the state (OAC 901:5-30-01)
classes.noxious: Prohibited noxious weed in Ohio: told by the township trustees that it's growing on the land, its owner or tenant must cut or destroy it within five days or show why there's no need, and road authorities must destroy it along roads; selling and planting it stay legal (OAC 901:5-37-01; ORC 5579.04, 5579.05)

jurisdictions.notes: Read 2026-10-31 under Jason's exception for official legal-code sites (codes.ohio.gov's robots.txt turns away all automated readers): only the pages named, with the honest user agent, at least 6 seconds apart; every request answered 200. Phase-in, OAC 901:5-30-01(C): the ban did not apply to Pyrus calleryana until January 7, 2023, or to Ligustrum vulgare until January 1, 2026; both dates have passed. The rule was first effective January 7, 2018; this version took effect February 13, 2023. Exceptions in the same rule: reed canary grass sold for use as animal feed (C)(3); disposing of a listed plant, controlling it, or using it for research or education under a department compliance agreement, in a way that does not spread it (D). The director may exempt a cultivar if scientific evidence shows it is not invasive (F); the rule names none. Purple loosestrife: ORC 927.682 forbids selling, offering for sale or planting Lythrum salicaria plants or seed without the director's permit; permits may be issued for controlled experiments, and the director must by rule exempt any variety shown not to threaten the environment. I found no such exemption rule. It is on the invasive list too, whose line (the same ban, and more) is the one shown; a plant on two lines takes the first. Multiflora rose: ORC 927.681 forbids selling, offering for sale or planting "any variety of multiflora rose plants or seed" without a permit, except that a licensed nurseryman may plant it as rootstock for other roses. The statute gives only the common name, so it adds no entry; Rosa multiflora is on the invasive list. Despite the name, OAC 901:5-37-01 and ORC 5579 do not forbid selling or planting a "prohibited noxious weed": the duties are to cut or destroy it on the township's notice (ORC 5579.05, 5579.06) and along roads (5579.04, 5579.08), so that class is listed. The noxious class is read from https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/rule-901:5-37-01 (effective February 16, 2025) and https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/chapter-5579. Left out of the noxious class: grapevines (Vitis spp.), listed only "when growing in groups of one hundred or more and not pruned, sprayed, cultivated, or otherwise maintained for two consecutive years"; a whole-genus entry would mark every garden grape. Also left out: Phyllostachys aureasculata (yellow groove bamboo), listed only "when the plant has spread from its original premise of planting and is not being maintained", which a planted, kept bamboo isn't; and Sorghum bicolor ("shatter cane", in both the rule and ORC 5579.04(A)) and Pastinaca sativa ("wild parsnip"), whose common names mean the weedy forms, so read whole they would take in grain sorghum and the garden parsnip. Salsola kali var. tenuifolia is the statute's own Russian thistle (ORC 5579.04(A)); the rule lists Russian thistle as Salsola tragus. Both are entered. ORC 5579.05 also reaches "wild parsnip, wild carrot, oxeye daisy, wild mustard, or other harmful weeds"; wild carrot, oxeye daisy and wild mustard are common names only and add no entries. Misspellings as printed: "Hesperis matronlis" and "Marsilea guadrifolia" (OAC 901:5-30-01); "Persicaria perfoliate" (OAC 901:5-37-01). Written in the catalog's form: "ssp." (OAC 901:5-30-01) and "sub." ("Lepidium draba sub. draba", OAC 901:5-37-01) as "subsp."; "Typha x glauca" and "Sorghum x almum" with the × sign. ORC 901.50 authorizes the invasive plant rule, OAC 901:5-30-02 creates its advisory committee, and ORC 927.51 holds nursery-stock definitions; none of them lists plants. Not included: Ohio's seed-law noxious weed seed lists, and pest quarantines or plant-pest orders under ORC 927.70 and 927.71, which were not read. Kew's accepted names, checked in its checklist (2026-10-31): Calystegia sepium, Conyza canadensis, Egeria densa, Eichhornia azurea, Fallopia japonica, Ficaria verna, Monochoria hastata and M. vaginalis, and Senecio glabellus Poir. (cressleaf groundsel; not the later homonym of S.Y.Hu) are homotypic synonyms of Convolvulus sepium, Erigeron canadensis, Elodea densa, Pontederia azurea, Reynoutria japonica, Ranunculus ficaria, Pontederia hastata and P. vaginalis, and Packera glabella. Kew writes crack willow as a hybrid, Salix × fragilis, and "Salix fragilis" only as a misapplied name, so it is matched by its printed name only. Hedge bindweed carries the background note it has on the Arkansas and Texas lists.

background.note: Background: hedge bindweed is hard to get rid of: it can regrow from any piece of rhizome left in the ground.

jurisdictions.title: Indiana's prohibited invasive plants (312 IAC 18-3-23, -25), Lythrum and multiflora rose (18-3-13), kudzu (18-3-16) and detrimental plants (IC 15-16-8)
jurisdictions.edition: Indiana Administrative Code, Title 312, Article 18, as readopted filed March 25, 2025 (20250423-IR-312240574RFA): 18-3-25 as filed March 18, 2019, 18-3-23 as amended May 9, 2019; the Indiana Register's current edition, as shown 2026-10-31; Indiana Code 15-16-7 and 15-16-8 as in the General Assembly's 2025 Indiana Code (15-16-8-1 last amended by P.L.13-2019)

classes.terrestrial: Prohibited invasive plant in Indiana: no one may sell it, offer or grow it for sale, give, barter, exchange or distribute it, move it or introduce it, but under a permit from the state entomologist (312 IAC 18-3-25)
classes.aquatic: Prohibited invasive aquatic plant in Indiana: no one may sell it, offer it for sale, give, barter, exchange or distribute it, or carry it by boat, vehicle or any other means, but under a permit from the state entomologist (312 IAC 18-3-23)
classes.lythrum: Prohibited in Indiana: no seeds or plants of any Lythrum species may be sold, offered for sale, given away or otherwise distributed; native species only under a permit, for an approved project (312 IAC 18-3-13)
classes.multiflora: Prohibited in Indiana: no one may plant it, but a certified nursery, as grafting stock for roses (312 IAC 18-3-13)
classes.kudzu: Prohibited in Indiana: no one may sell, distribute, offer, give away, barter, exchange or plant any part of it (312 IAC 18-3-16)
classes.detrimental: Detrimental plant in Indiana: whoever owns or possesses land must destroy it before it matures, by cutting, mowing, plowing or chemicals; growing and selling it as a plant aren't banned (IC 15-16-8-1, -3, -14)

jurisdictions.notes: Read in Jason's own Chrome browser (Claude in Chrome), with his OK: the Indiana Register's site shows its text only to a browser, and its data service refuses other readers (403), so nothing was fetched outside the browser. Each section's text was copied from the page into catalog-src/legal/in-312-18-3-<n>.txt and checked against a SHA-256 hash the browser computed from the page itself (all match). 18-3-25's bans on selling and moving took effect one year after the section did (it was filed March 18, 2019): long past. Names: "Hygrophilia polysperma" is printed for Hygrophila polysperma; "Lonicera x bella" and "Reynoutria x bohemica" are written with the hybrid sign; "Phragmites australis subspecies australis" is the subspecies only (the native subspecies americanus is not listed); "Dioscorea polystachya (oppositifolia)" is entered as D. polystachya. Lythrum: 18-3-13(c) covers "any species of Lythrum (commonly known as purple loosestrife)": entered as the genus, natives included, since (e) lets native species be sold only under a permit. Rosa multiflora: 18-3-13(b) forbids planting it, not selling it; a certified nursery may plant it as grafting stock (d). Left out: Caulerpa taxifolia and Nitellopsis obtusa, algae. Detrimental plants: IC 15-16-8-1's list (the same plants as 15-16-7-2's noxious weeds, which bind only where a county has a weed control board), read the same way in Jason's Chrome from the General Assembly's site and checked against the browser's hash (whitespace normalized: catalog-src/legal/in-ic-15-16-7-8.txt). Every owner or possessor of land must destroy them before they mature (15-16-8-3); knowingly selling Canada thistle seed is an infraction (15-16-8-14(a)(5)); otherwise selling or growing them isn't banned, so listed. Its item (13), "in residential areas only, noxious weeds and rank vegetation", names no plant. Shattercane is printed "Sorghum bicolor (L.) Moench spp. drummondii (Steud.) deWet": the subspecies, not grain sorghum. "Sorghum almum" is written with the hybrid sign. Bur cucumber, horseweed, tall waterhemp and smooth pigweed are natives the statute names. Not read: the pest and disease rules of 312 IAC 18-3 (black stem rust's Berberis and Mahonia rules regulate nursery stock as hosts of a disease, not as weeds). Kew's accepted names, checked in its checklist (2026-10-31): Egeria densa, Eichhornia azurea, Monochoria hastata and M. vaginalis, and Polygonum perfoliatum are homotypic synonyms of Elodea densa, Pontederia azurea, Pontederia hastata and P. vaginalis, and Persicaria perfoliata; Achyranthes japonica, Humulus japonicus and Salvinia herzogii are heterotypic synonyms of Achyranthes bidentata, Humulus scandens and Salvinia biloba, and are matched as those species. Kew makes Pueraria lobata a variety (Pueraria montana var. lobata), so it is matched by its printed name only.

jurisdictions.title: Illinois exotic weeds (17 Ill. Adm. Code 1100; 525 ILCS 10) and noxious weeds (8 Ill. Adm. Code 220; 505 ILCS 100)
jurisdictions.edition: 17 Ill. Adm. Code 1100 as adopted at 49 Ill. Reg. 12989, effective October 1, 2025; Illinois Exotic Weeds Act, 525 ILCS 10, as amended by P.A. 103-620, eff. 1-1-25; 8 Ill. Adm. Code 220 as amended at 26 Ill. Reg. 14644, effective September 23, 2002; Illinois Noxious Weed Law, 505 ILCS 100 (Illinois General Assembly and its Joint Committee on Administrative Rules)

classes.exotic: Exotic weed in Illinois: its seeds, plants or plant parts may not be bought, sold, offered for sale, distributed or planted without a permit from the Department of Natural Resources (525 ILCS 10/4; 17 Ill. Adm. Code 1100.30, 1100.40)
classes.exotic2028: Exotic weed in Illinois from January 1, 2028: from then its seeds, plants or plant parts may not be bought, sold, offered for sale, distributed or planted without a permit from the Department of Natural Resources (525 ILCS 10/4; 17 Ill. Adm. Code 1100.30, 1100.40)
classes.noxious: Noxious weed in Illinois: every person must control its spread and eradicate it on land they own or control (505 ILCS 100/3; 8 Ill. Adm. Code 220.10, 220.60)
classes.noxiousTown: Noxious weed within the corporate limits of Illinois cities, villages and incorporated towns: there, every person must control its spread and eradicate it on land they own or control (505 ILCS 100/3; 8 Ill. Adm. Code 220.10, 220.60)

jurisdictions.notes: Since P.A. 103-620 (eff. 1-1-25) the Act names no plants: Section 3 leaves the list to the Department of Natural Resources' rules, and the list is 17 Ill. Adm. Code 1100.30. The rule says: "Name of plant species vary for the same species and can change. Updates of nomenclature do not remove the exotic weed designation of a species." Phase-in: callery pear, Pyrus calleryana, is listed "starting January 1, 2028": until then it is listed, not banned; from that date its class should become exotic, tier ban. Permits (1100.40) are only to sell or distribute non-viable material, or to plant viable material to study control in a controlled environment or as biological control in the wild. The Act exempts commercial propagation of exotic weeds for sale outside Illinois, certified under the Insect Pest and Plant Disease Act (525 ILCS 10/4(b)). Violations are a Class B misdemeanor, and exotic weeds offered for sale may be confiscated and destroyed (525 ILCS 10/5); a municipality may order them eradicated on all property within its limits (10/4(d)). The rule exempts no varieties. Dipsacus spp. and Tamarix spp. are entered as genera; the rule prints "Reynoutria x bohemica", entered with the × sign. Noxious weeds: 505 ILCS 100 and Part 220 set a duty to control and eradicate them (505 ILCS 100/3; 220.10), and forbid moving articles infested with them, nursery stock and sod included, until cleaned (220.230); they do not forbid selling or planting the plants, so listed. Giant ragweed and common ragweed are noxious only "within the corporate limits of cities, villages, and incorporated towns": class noxiousTown; both are native. Marihuana, Cannabis sativa: the Act's definition of noxious weed "does not include industrial hemp as defined and authorized under the Industrial Hemp Act" (505 ILCS 100/2). Read narrower than printed: "Perennial members of the sorghum genus, including johnsongrass (Sorghum halepense), sorghum almum, and other johnsongrass X sorghum crosses with rhizomes" as Sorghum halepense and Sorghum × almum (printed "sorghum almum"); the genus is not entered, since its annual members (grain sorghum) are not listed, and the unnamed "johnsongrass X sorghum crosses with rhizomes" are left out. Kudzu is on both lists, printed "Pueraria labata" in 220.60 ("Pueraria lobata" in 220.210) and "Pueraria montana" in 1100.30: shown as exotic only; check that Pueraria montana matches the catalog's kudzu (Kew: Pueraria montana var. lobata). Left out: seed-law lists and advisory lists (for example the Illinois Invasive Species Council's). Kew's accepted name, checked in its checklist (2026-10-31): Ficaria verna is a homotypic synonym of Ranunculus ficaria.

jurisdictions.title: West Virginia noxious weeds (61CSR14A; W. Va. Code §§19-12-14, 19-12D) and the white pine blister rust quarantine on black currant
jurisdictions.edition: 61CSR14A, Noxious Weeds Rule, filed April 13, 2023, effective May 1, 2023 (Secretary of State, Code of State Rules); W. Va. Code chapter 19, articles 12 (Plant Pest Act) and 12D (Noxious Weed Act), as published on code.wvlegislature.gov, printed November 1, 2026 (UTC); Department of Agriculture's Barberry and Black Stem Rust Quarantine of May 11, 1992, and White Pine Blister Rust Quarantine, established October 19, 1967, amended May 11, 1992

classes.noxious: Noxious weed in West Virginia: it may not be sold, offered for sale, or moved, shipped or delivered into or within the state without a permit from the Commissioner of Agriculture (W. Va. Code §§19-12-14, 19-12D-7; 61CSR14A §5.1)
classes.barberry: Noxious weed in West Virginia: it may not be sold, offered for sale, or moved, shipped or delivered into or within the state without a permit from the Commissioner of Agriculture, who may exempt cultivated varieties found to be sterile (W. Va. Code §§19-12-14, 19-12D-7; 61CSR14A §5.2)
classes.multiflora: Noxious weed in West Virginia by statute: it may not be brought or moved into the state, sold, offered or exposed for sale, or kept to sell, and no permit may ever be granted for its sale or its movement into the state (W. Va. Code §§19-12D-5, 19-12D-12)
classes.federal: Federal noxious weed adopted as a West Virginia noxious weed: it may not be sold, offered for sale, or moved, shipped or delivered into or within the state without a permit from the Commissioner of Agriculture (61CSR14A §5.4 and Appendix A; W. Va. Code §§19-12-14, 19-12D-7)
classes.blackCurrant: European black currant in West Virginia: a white pine blister rust quarantine says it may not be moved to any destination in the state (White Pine Blister Rust Quarantine §II; W. Va. Code §19-12-6)

jurisdictions.notes: Read 2026-10-31. The Secretary of State publishes 61CSR14A as a scanned PDF of the final filing (filed April 13, 2023, effective May 1, 2023, authorized by SB 361, passed March 11, 2023; sunset August 1, 2033). Its text was read from the Word file of the same filing on the same page, and checked against the scan: section 5 by eye, Appendix A by OCR (the same names). The rule declares the plants; the statutes say what may not be done with them. W. Va. Code §19-12-14 (Plant Pest Act): no person may sell, barter, expose, offer for sale, or move, transport, deliver, ship or offer for shipment into or within the state any noxious weed in any living stage without a federal permit, where applicable, or a state permit, which may be issued only if it is not injurious, is generally present already, or is for scientific purposes under safeguards; read at https://code.wvlegislature.gov/pdf/19-12/. §19-12D-7(b) (Noxious Weed Act) likewise forbids moving it into or within the state without a permit. Violations are misdemeanors (§19-12-16; §19-12D-11). Japanese barberry (§5.2): the Commissioner may exempt cultivated varieties found sterile and of no threat to agriculture; neither the rule nor the Department of Agriculture's in-state nursery page names any exempted cultivar. The Department's news release of June 2, 2020 said its sale became illegal on July 1, 2020, after a phase-in for existing stock under the 2018 rule (not read); the 2023 rule has no phase-in, so the ban is in force. Multiflora rose: declared a noxious weed by statute (§19-12D-5(b)); §19-12D-12 makes importing, bringing or moving it into the state, or selling, offering or exposing it for sale, or possessing it with intent to sell, a misdemeanor, and forbids the Commissioner to grant any permit for its sale or its movement into the state. The Department's in-state nursery page says garden roses grafted or budded onto multiflora rootstock may be shipped into the state; the statute names no such exception. Federal list: §5.4 adopts the Federal Noxious Weed List as an extension of the state list and prints it as Appendix A, 'as of November 10, 2010'. It is entered as printed (class federal), not by reference to the US entry, because it is a dated list whose names differ from the current CFR's in places: Digitaria scalarum, Mimosa invisa and Homeria spp. are printed, and Cuscuta jepsonii, C. nevadensis and C. occidentalis are among the excepted dodders. The Cuscuta exceptions are entered as printed; five are misspelled ('ceanothii', 'cephalanthii', 'corylii', 'exalta', 'vetchii'), and their correct spellings, as the US entry has them, are in exceptAlso. Left out: Caulerpa taxifolia, an alga. 'Avena sterilis Linnaeus (including Avena ludoviciana Durieu)': both entered, as in the US entry. Sagittaria sagittifolia is printed twice: entered once. 'Rubus fruticosus Linnaeus (complex)': entered as the one species. Printed with capitals, entered lower-case: 'L. Morrowii' (Lonicera morrowii), 'Inula Britannica', 'Onopordum Illyricum'. Abbreviated genera written out: 'C. crispus' and 'C. nutans' (Carduus), 'P. cuspidatum' (Polygonum), 'L. Morrowii' (Lonicera). Misspelled, with the correct spelling in kew: 'Elaeagnus umbellate', 'Lonicera tartarica', 'Carthamus oxyacantha' (as the US entry has it), 'Setaria pallide-fusca' (hyphen dropped). For the reviewer, names Kew files under other accepted names: Polygonum cuspidatum, Polygonum perfoliatum, Pueraria thunbergiana (kudzu; Kew: Pueraria montana var. lobata), and in the appendix the names the US entry reviewed. Narcotic plants: §19-12D-8(c) lets the Commissioner help destroy 'marijuana or hemp, Cannabis spp., or other plants which produce drugs which have been condemned for destruction under the narcotics laws' and says 'Such drug producing plants are hereby declared noxious'; rule §5.3 is 'reserved for narcotic drug producing plants' and names none. Read as reaching only plants condemned under the narcotics laws, so there is no Cannabis or Papaver entry; the Department's nursery page lists marijuana ('Canabis sativa') and opium poppy (Papaver somniferum) among noxious weeds, but no statute or rule read names the opium poppy, and hemp is licensed under the Industrial Hemp rule (61CSR29, not read). Quarantines: orders of the Commissioner under W. Va. Code §19-12-6, which 61CSR14 §2.14 names ('White Pine Blister Rust Quarantine, Black Stem Rust Quarantine') and whose violation its Table 61-14-A fines; read from the Department's PDFs, https://agriculture.wv.gov/wp-content/uploads/WV_Black_Stem_Rust_Quarantine.pdf (May 11, 1992) and https://agriculture.wv.gov/wp-content/uploads/WV_Blister_Rust_Quarantine.pdf (1967, amended May 11, 1992). Black stem rust: all species and varieties of Berberis, Mahonia and Mahoberberis are considered rust-susceptible, and prohibited, except those the USDA designates rust-resistant or immune (§§IV, VI); the quarantine names none, so the three genera are entered whole with no exceptions, though the USDA's list (not read) exempts many species and cultivars: the class line states the exception, but a 'every Berberis species' line would overstate it. Japanese barberry is entered first as a noxious weed and takes that line. Blister rust: European black currant (Ribes nigrum) may not be moved to any destination in the state (§II), entered before the genus. Every other currant and gooseberry (Ribes, natives included): 'dissemination, growing or other uses' are prohibited only in the 23 counties the quarantine names (§I), where the Commissioner may destroy them (cultivated species other than European black currant only within 1,500 feet of white pine stands, §III); tiered listed because the ban does not reach the rest of the state and the app cannot tell counties apart, though inside those counties it is a ban. Not law, left out: the seed law and its noxious weed seed list (61CSR9; W. Va. Code chapter 19, article 16) and advisory lists. Checked, no plant list: 61CSR14 (Plant Pest Act rule), the active rules of the Division of Natural Resources (title 58), and the gypsy moth quarantine (an insect pest). Reviewer (2026-10-31): left out, as other states' host-plant quarantines are: the Barberry and Black Stem Rust Quarantine, whose ban on every Berberis, Mahonia and Mahoberberis excepts those the USDA designates rust-resistant without naming them (genus entries would cover the resistant barberries and mahonias most gardens have); and the blister rust quarantine's ban on every Ribes in 23 named counties (county-limited, as Virginia's box tree moth quarantine). Kept: the same quarantine's statewide ban on moving European black currant. Kew's accepted names (2026-10-31): the appendix's federal names as the US entry records them, checked there; and Polygonum cuspidatum and Polygonum perfoliatum, Kew's Reynoutria japonica (heterotypic) and Persicaria perfoliata (homotypic). Pueraria thunbergiana and Setaria pallidefusca, which Kew makes a variety and a subspecies (Pueraria montana var. lobata, Setaria pumila subsp. pallidefusca), are matched by their printed names only.

jurisdictions.title: Alabama noxious weeds (Ala. Admin. Code r. 80-10-14) and nonindigenous aquatic plants (r. 220-2-.124)

classes.classA: Class A noxious weed in Alabama: moving it, or anything infested with it, into or within the state is prohibited, except under the rule's certificates and permits (Ala. Admin. Code r. 80-10-14-.04, 80-10-14-.05)

jurisdictions.notes: Noxious weeds (Department of Agriculture and Industries, 80-10-14): the rule prohibits "The movement of Class A, B, or C noxious weeds or any regulated article infested with Class A, B, or C noxious weeds into or within Alabama", "Except as permitted in 80-10-14-.07 and 80-10-14-.08" (80-10-14-.05(1)). It does not mention sale or planting; all three classes are tiered ban because it forbids moving the plants into or within the state. Permit exceptions: scientific permits "to allow the movement of noxious weeds in any living stage and any regulated articles for scientific purposes" (.08(3)); limited permits for "noncertified regulated articles" (a regulated article includes "Any noxious weed", .02(13)) to specified destinations for limited handling, utilization, processing or treatment when the inspector finds no hazard of spread (.08(2)); and the nursery rule's special permits for the entrance of "noxious weeds that are needed for experimental purposes" (80-10-1-.11(2)). Certificates (.08(1)) are for articles found free of noxious weeds. Inspectors may seize, treat or dispose of articles moving in violation (.10); "Evidence of noxious weed shall be considered a public nuisance" (.02(12)); violations carry the penalties of Code of Ala. 1975, §2-25-22 (.12). Class A item (a) is "All weeds listed in 7 C.F.R. 360.200 Federal Noxious Weed List, the same of which is hereby incorporated by reference herein including its subsequent amendments and editions" (also .13): so this list adopts the US entry's plants into Class A, by reference; its own entries come first. Printed misspellings, with Kew's spelling given: "Althernanthera philoxeroides", "Potamgeton crispus", "Eichornia crassipes", "Stratlotes aloides". Fatoua villosa is printed with the common names "Hairy crabgrass, mulberry weed": entered by its botanical name. Phragmites australis is printed as the whole species, the native American subspecies too. Nonindigenous aquatic plants (Department of Conservation and Natural Resources, 220-2-.124, amended effective October 15, 2026; text in chapter 220-2, https://admincode.legislature.state.al.us/api/chapter/220-2): the rule lists the plants "which are prohibited by Section 9-20-3 from being introduced or placed or caused to be introduced or placed into public waters of the state". It forbids nothing else (selling, growing or moving them, or planting outside public waters), so listed. The Alabama Nonindigenous Aquatic Plant Control Act itself (Code of Ala. 1975, §§9-20-1 to 9-20-7) was not read: its only official online text is the Legislature's browser application; the class sentence is worded from the rule. Penalty: §9-20-6. Left out of the aquatic class: Lyngbya wollei (a cyanobacterium, not a plant); 11 printed plants that are also in 80-10-14's classes, where they show as banned (Alternanthera philoxeroides, printed "Alternanthera philoxeriodes"; Egeria densa; Potamogeton crispus; Myriophyllum spicatum; Eichhornia crassipes; Myriophyllum aquaticum; Lythrum salicaria; Najas minor; Stratiotes aloides; Pistia stratiotes; Trapa natans); and 6 that are federal noxious weeds, so Class A in Alabama by reference and shown by the federal entry (Salvinia molesta, Hydrilla verticillata, Hygrophila polysperma, Limnophila sessiliflora, Eichhornia azurea, Ipomoea aquatica, printed "Ipomea aquatica"). "Lagarosiphon spp" is entered as the genus; its one federal species, Lagarosiphon major, is also Class A by reference. Nymphoides cristata is printed "(synonym N. hydrophylla)". Left out: the seed rules (80-11), with their own noxious weed seed lists; the nursery rules (80-10-1), which name no plants; the pest and disease quarantines on host plants (80-10-4, -5, -7, -10, -15, -19, -20), not read; and the boll weevil rule that non-commercial cotton "shall not be planted in an elimination area without a waiver" (80-10-12-.11(3)), since the rule that set out the elimination area (80-10-12-.05) was repealed effective 9/24/07. Advisory lists (for example the Alabama Invasive Plant Council's) are not law. Not read: the Alabama Plant Pest Act (Code of Ala. 1975, Title 2, Chapter 25), the authority for 80-10-14 (§2-25-4), whose official online text is the same browser application. Kew's accepted names (2026-10-31): Egeria densa, Eichornia crassipes (Eichhornia), Landoltia punctata and Polygonum perfoliatum are homotypic synonyms of Elodea densa, Pontederia crassipes, Spirodela punctata and Persicaria perfoliata; Polygonum cuspidatum, Ludwigia uruguayensis and Nymphoides cristata are heterotypic synonyms of Reynoutria japonica, Ludwigia grandiflora and Nymphoides hydrophyllum, and are matched as those species.

jurisdictions.notes: Part 413 lets the Commission of Agriculture and Rural Development add or delete plant species by order (MCL 324.41302(1)). The Commission's Invasive Species Order Amendment No. 1 of 2026 (effective May 20, 2026; read from the copy Jason saved from michigan.gov, which refuses automated readers: https://www.michigan.gov/mdard/-/media/Project/Websites/mdard/documents/boards/agcommission/2026-Invasive-Species-Order.pdf) adds water hyacinth, printed "Water-hyacinth (Eichhornia crassipes)", and water lettuce (Pistia stratiotes) to the prohibited species, "30 days after this order is signed", so from June 19, 2026; and Japanese barberry (Berberis thunbergii), glossy buckthorn (Frangula alnus), Callery pear (Pyrus calleryana) and common buckthorn (Rhamnus cathartica) to the restricted species: "sale and cultivation of these species will be allowed in 2026 and 2027. Restriction of these species begins January 1, 2028" (class restricted2028, listed until then; on that date they move to restricted, a ban). The order excepts no cultivars. It amends a standing Invasive Species Order, which with any earlier amendments (a 2015 order on water soldier, Stratiotes aloides, is reported) was not read and may list more plants. The statute's lists are entered as printed. Each listed plant includes "a hybrid or genetically engineered variant of the species" and, for terrestrial plants, "a fragment, including a seed or other propagule" (324.41301(1)(k), (o)): the species are recorded; the hybrids are not entered (so Bohemian knotweed, a Japanese knotweed hybrid, is covered by the statute but not matched). Prohibited and restricted plants carry the same duties; they differ in the fines (324.41309) and in one exception: an aquatic restricted species may be possessed as a department order under 324.41302(6) allows for naturalized organisms. Possession does not include plants merely present on one's land unless one knowingly introduced them, plants kept only where they were found in the wild, or plants held to be promptly destroyed (324.41301(2)). "Introduce" is to "stock, place, plant, release, or allow the release" at a location "where the organism is not already naturalized" (324.41301(1)(f)); permits to introduce a plant are the Department of Agriculture and Rural Development's (324.41305(b)). Purple loosestrife: "cultivars of purple loosestrife developed and recognized to be sterile and approved by the director of the department of agriculture and rural development under section 16a of the insect pest and plant disease act, 1931 PA 189, MCL 286.216a, are not a restricted species"; MCL 286.216a and the list of approved cultivars were not read. Japanese knotweed is printed "Fallopia japonica" and listed as prohibited. Phragmites: printed "Phragmites or common reed (Phragmites australis)" with no exception for the native subspecies (americanus), though a restricted species must be "not native" (324.41302(3)(b)); recorded as printed: the reviewer should decide whether to narrow it. Giant salvinia is printed "Salvinia molesta, auriculata, biloba, or herzogii": four entries. Left out of the prohibited list: cylindro (Cylindrospermopsis raciborskii), a cyanobacterium, and starry stonewort (Nitellopsis obtusa), an alga; and the non-plant species. Noxious weeds (1941 PA 359): the landowner's duty is to destroy them; the act forbids no sale or planting, so listed. It does not apply to weeds in small-grain fields (247.64(4)); a county, city, township or village may add "any other plant" it regards as a common nuisance (247.62(1)(l)), not entered; "Noxious weeds does not include milkweed (any species of the genus Asclepias)" (247.62(2)). Read narrower than printed: "Mustards (charlock, black mustard, and Indian mustard, species of the genus Brassica or Sinapis)" as charlock, Sinapis arvensis; black mustard, Brassica nigra; and Indian mustard, Brassica juncea (the mustard-greens crop); the genera are not entered, which would take in cabbage and its kin. Recorded as printed, for the reviewer: "Wild carrot (Daucus carota)": the species includes the garden carrot, which the act does not except; "Ragweed (Ambrosia elatior L.)", entered without the author. Dodders: "any species of the genus Cuscuta", natives included. Natives on the noxious list: the native dodders, common ragweed, poison ivy and poison sumac. Giant hogweed is on both lists: shown as prohibited. Left out: the seed law's noxious weed seed lists (1965 PA 329), the departments' watch list and other advisory lists, and pest quarantines on host plants. Reviewer (2026-10-31): left out of the noxious weeds: "Mustards (charlock, black mustard, and Indian mustard, species of the genus Brassica or Sinapis)", whose species are named by common name only (the genera would take in cabbage and its kin); and "Wild carrot (Daucus carota)", whose species takes in the garden carrot, as Ohio's and Pennsylvania's wild parsnip and shattercane are left out. Kew's accepted names (2026-10-31): Fallopia japonica, Eichhornia azurea, Eichhornia crassipes, Egeria densa, Monochoria hastata and M. vaginalis, Polygonum perfoliatum and Salvinia herzogii as Reynoutria japonica, Pontederia azurea, Pontederia crassipes, Elodea densa, Pontederia hastata and P. vaginalis, Persicaria perfoliata and Salvinia biloba; Ambrosia elatior, a heterotypic synonym of Ambrosia artemisiifolia, is matched as that species.

jurisdictions.edition: P.L.2025, c.290 (S1029 2R SCS), approved January 20, 2026, effective immediately (New Jersey Legislature's chapter law); N.J.A.C. 2:20-2 as posted by the Department of Agriculture (effective July 27, 2000), amended at 50 N.J.R. 1887(a), effective August 20, 2018, readopted without change effective October 3, 2024

classes.prohibited: Prohibited invasive species in New Jersey: from early 2027 no one may propagate it in the state, or import or otherwise introduce it, and from early 2030 no one may sell, distribute, export or offer it or its seeds for sale, without a conditional use waiver from the Department of Environmental Protection (N.J.S.A. 23:2A-20)
classes.blackCurrant: European black currant in New Jersey: its cultivars and hybrids may be possessed or moved into or within the state only under a special permit from the Department of Agriculture, given for cultivars resistant or immune to white pine blister rust (N.J.A.C. 2:20-2.2, 2:20-2.3)

jurisdictions.notes: Invasive Species Management Act, P.L.2025, c.290, approved January 20, 2026, "This act shall take effect immediately" (§11). Its own list (§4a, N.J.S.A. 23:2A-20) names 30 plants; item (31) adds any species the Department of Environmental Protection lists by rule, and none has been adopted: the Act gives it 12 months (§7a), and the Department of Agriculture's page shows its rule, N.J.A.C. 2:19-3, as "(Coming Soon)". Phase-in: propagating, importing or otherwise introducing a listed plant is forbidden "Commencing on the first day of the 13th month next following the effective date" (§4b), counted here as February 1, 2027; selling, distributing, exporting or offering it or its seeds, from "the first day of the 49th month" (§4c), counted as February 1, 2030. The Department of Agriculture's page gives January 1, 2027 and January 1, 2030. Neither date has come on 2026-10-31, so the class is listed; from the first of these dates its tier should become ban. §4c begins "except as provided under P.L.1963, c.29 (C.4:8-17.13 et seq.)", a law not read. §4d applies the bans to "any non-hybrid sub-species, variety, cultivar, or other subcategory" of a species listed by rule. Waivers: a conditional use waiver is "an authorization issued by the Department of Environmental Protection that provides for a limited, specified use of a prohibited invasive species" (§3); its process is to be set by rule (§7a), and the Department of Agriculture's concurrence is sought for agricultural waivers. The Department of Agriculture enforces first for selling, offering, propagating for sale or importing; civil administrative penalties are $1,000 to $2,000 (§9). The Act supersedes contrary local ordinances (§8). Exempt cultivars (§4e), which must be labelled and sold with the Invasive Species Council's educational materials: Berberis thunbergii Aurea, UCONNBTCP4N, UCONNBTB113, UCONNBTB048 and UCONNBTB039; Miscanthus sinensis NCMS1 and Tift M77. The exemptions "shall expire two years after the effective date of this act" (January 20, 2028) unless continued by rule (§4f). Entries can't except cultivars, so the species are recorded whole. "running bamboo (Phyllostachys)" is entered as the genus; the Department of Agriculture's page prints "Phyllostachys species". That page also misprints "Humulus japonicas", "Lespedeza cuneate" and the porcelain berry as a subspecies; the statute's names are used. White pine blister rust (N.J.A.C. 2:20-2): read in the Department of Agriculture's posting of N.J.A.C. 2:20 (chapter effective July 27, 2000; file of September 15, 2005: https://www.nj.gov/agriculture/divisions/pi/pdf/AmendedFinal05-NJAC220Quarantines.pdf), with the amendment of 2:20-2.3 (50 N.J.R. 1887(a), effective August 20, 2018) and the readoption without change effective October 3, 2024 (56 N.J.R. 2139(c)). The online N.J.A.C. (LexisNexis) is, in the Office of Administrative Law's words, "not the official Code", and was not read; check the current text there. Black currant: "The possession or movement of plant cultivars and hybrids of European Black Currant (Ribes nigrum L.) into or within New Jersey is only allowed under special permit issued by the Department" (2.2(a)2); permits are for resistant or immune cultivars, which since 2018 need the source's certification and "favorable scientific review and certification of the varieties by the USDA APHIS and/or the U.S. Forest Service" (2.3(d)), and the 2005 text's list of four permitted cultivars (Consort, Coronet, Crusader, Titania) is gone. Hybrids of black currant (hybrids by parents) are not entered. Red currant and gooseberry: the posted text of 2.2(a)3 has no verb: "The possession or movement of red currant and gooseberry plants (Ribes sp. and Grossularia sp.) into or within New Jersey except the following municipalities, constituting a protective area: ..."; read with 2.2(a)4, "Currant plants and gooseberry plants other than the European Black Currant (Ribes nigrum L.) may be moved into and within all other points in New Jersey", it bars them from the protective area. An unofficial current copy shows 2.2(a) with no item 4. Tier listed, as it holds in eight municipalities only. Five-needled pines may be moved except when visibly infected (2.2(a)1): not entered. Left out: seed law (N.J.A.C. 2:21, the Department of Agriculture's noxious weed seed list); the pest quarantines of N.J.A.C. 2:20 (golden nematode, Asian longhorned beetle host plants moved out of quarantined areas, and others); advisory lists. No New Jersey noxious weed law beyond seed law was found. Reviewer (2026-10-31): the Act's dates are "the first day of the 13th month" and "of the 49th month" next following its approval on January 20, 2026: February 1, 2027 and February 1, 2030 by that count; the Department of Agriculture's page says January 1 of each year; the line says the years only. Listed until the first date, when its tier becomes ban. Left out: N.J.A.C. 2:20-2.2(a)3's protective area of eight municipalities (Ribes and Grossularia), municipality-limited, as Virginia's box tree moth quarantine. Kew's accepted names (2026-10-31): Humulus japonicus (heterotypic) as Humulus scandens, Photinia villosa (homotypic) as Pourthiaea villosa.

classes.aquatic: Prohibited aquatic plant in South Carolina: no one may possess, sell, offer for sale or import it, bring it into the state, or release or place it into any of the state's waters, but under a special import permit for research (S.C. Code §50-13-1415)

Code Regs. 27-135, 27-161; Clemson University, July 14, 2021)

jurisdictions.notes: Plant pests: S.C. Code Regs. 27-135 names no plants. It says "The official listing of plant pests in SC shall be maintained and made publicly available on Clemson's website" (27-135(3)), and the Department of Plant Industry's list page says "This page shall serve as the official listing of plant pests in accordance with South Carolina Code of Regulations Chapter 27 Article 10". The page is undated; it was read on October 31, 2026, and only its plant table is entered (the rest lists insects, diseases and other pests). What the law prints: the Director may "determine and implement appropriate measures to eradicate, control, or slow the spread of plant pests" (27-135(1)); a nursery's inspection "must reveal that ... the Nursery Stock is sufficiently free from Plant Pests" (27-161(B), 27-162(B)); plants entering the state "found infested with Plant Pests shall be declared a public nuisance" (27-163(D)(2)); and the Commission may "seize, quarantine, treat, or otherwise dispose of the plant pest, host, or article" (S.C. Code §46-9-60(A)) and stop the sale of plant material sold or grown in violation (§46-33-100). Neither the regulation, the statutes read, nor the list page says a listed plant may not be sold, planted or moved, so by the law's own words the class would be listed. The Department of Plant Industry says otherwise: its news release of July 14, 2021 (not law) says "Typically, when a species is added to the State Plant Pest List, the change goes into effect immediately and it becomes illegal to move or sell it that same day", and that the listing of Pyrus calleryana, Elaeagnus umbellata, Elaeagnus angustifolia and Elaeagnus pungens "will make them illegal to sell or trade within South Carolina" but "it will not be illegal to possess them", with "The ban on sales" beginning October 1, 2024 (a date already past) and covering "Bradford pear trees and any other pear trees grown on the commonly used Pyrus calleryana rootstock". The South Carolina Noxious Weed Act (S.C. Code §§46-23-10 to -90) lets the Director designate noxious weeds and the Commission seize or quarantine those new to or not widely prevalent in the state; its one prohibition is on moving a noxious weed out of a county the Commission has quarantined for it (§46-23-40(c)). No separate noxious weed list and no such county quarantine were found. Entered as printed, with authors dropped ("(Mart.) Griscb.", "R. Brown", "H.B.K.", "Trin."). "Avena sterilis, A. ludoviciana" is two entries. "Indula brittanica" is printed for Inula britannica. The Orobanche exceptions are printed with the genus abbreviated ("O. bulbosa" ...) and two misspelled, "O. fasciculate" and "O. uniflorum": entered as printed, with the federal list's spellings, Orobanche fasciculata and Orobanche uniflora, as exceptAlso. Left out: Caulerpa taxifolia, an alga; and "Cuscuta spp.", printed "Dodders, with some exceptions" without naming them (the federal entry shows Cuscuta with its exceptions). Read as printed: Phragmites australis, the whole species, native American subspecies too. Prohibited aquatic plants: S.C. Code §50-13-1415 says "No person shall possess, sell, offer for sale, import, bring, or cause to be brought or imported into this State, or release or place into any waters of this State any of the following plants: (1) Water Hyacinth (2) Hydrilla Provided, however, that the department may issue special import permits to qualified persons for research purposes only." "Hydrilla" is entered as the genus Hydrilla, the printed word. "Water Hyacinth" is a common name only and is not entered; Eichhornia crassipes, which the plant pest list calls "Water hyacinth", shows in the pest class. The section lets the department add species by regulation; none was found in the Department of Natural Resources' regulations (chapter 123). The Department of Environmental Services' "illegal aquatic plants" page and flyer are not law and were not used. Not entered, because the rules name the plants by common name only (for the reviewer to decide): currant and gooseberry plants, which "No person, firm, or corporation shall knowingly plant ... within any such Blister Rust Control Area unless a special permit shall have been issued", nor move there from elsewhere in the state, and which may be destroyed there as a public nuisance (27-11); Clemson's regulated-areas page puts Spartanburg, Greenville, Pickens and Oconee counties in the area. And cotton: "Non-commercial or ornamental cotton shall not be planted without the prior written approval of the Director" (27-1096(C)), and "ornamental cottonseed" and "individual potted specimens of cotton plants" are "prohibited from sale or distribution within the state" (27-1099(B)). Left out: the witchweed quarantine (27-40 to 27-50; Striga is on the plant pest list and the federal list), which requires a certificate or permit to move it out of the regulated area, Horry and Marion counties; the other pest and disease rules on host plants (tomato and tobacco transplants, 27-20, 27-30; Asian longhorned beetle, 27-58; sweetpotato weevil, 27-60 ff.; plum pox virus, 27-75, which bars planting Prunus for a year after eradication in a quarantined area, none at present; light brown apple moth, Phytophthora ramorum and citrus greening, 27-77 to 27-79; phony peach, 27-80; Japanese beetle, 27-100 ff.; imported fire ant, 27-120 ff.; Asian citrus psyllid, 27-137; seed Irish potatoes and sweet potatoes, 27-140, 27-150); seed certification and seed rules with noxious weed seed limits; and advisory lists. The Legislature's Code of Regulations is unannotated and says it "is not official"; it is current through State Register Volume 50, Issue 3 (effective March 27, 2026). Violations: misdemeanor (S.C. Code §46-9-90(A); §46-23-80). Reviewer (2026-10-31): tiered ban by the agency's reading, Jason's decision (2026-10-31: "Flag them red, and say something along the lines of 'by agency reading'"). No regulation or statute read says a listed plant may not be sold; Clemson University's news release of July 14, 2021 (saved: sc-clemson-news-194130) says "Typically, when a species is added to the State Plant Pest List, the change goes into effect immediately and it becomes illegal to move or sell it that same day", that the ban on selling Callery pear (and pears grown on its rootstock) and three Elaeagnus began October 1, 2024, and that keeping plants already owned stays legal. Left out: Oryza sativa (printed "Red Rice and Asian rice") and Citrus reticulata var. unshu (Satsuma), crops whose listing the list doesn't explain; read whole they'd mark rice and satsumas as banned, as Ohio's shattercane and wild parsnip are left out. Kew's accepted names (2026-10-31), by which these are also matched: Calonyction muricatum as Ipomoea muricata; Centaurea repens as Rhaponticum repens; Cnicus benedictus as Centaurea benedicta; Egeria densa as Elodea densa; Eichhornia azurea as Pontederia azurea; Eichhornia crassipes as Pontederia crassipes; Emex australis as Rumex hypogaeus; Emex spinosa as Rumex spinosus; Euphorbia prunifolia as Euphorbia heterophylla; Ficaria verna as Ranunculus ficaria; Indula brittanica as Pentanema britannica; Leptochloa chinensis as Dinebra chinensis; Ludwigia uruguayensis as Ludwigia grandiflora; Monochoria hastata as Pontederia hastata; Monochoria vaginalis as Pontederia vaginalis; Nymphoides cristata as Nymphoides hydrophyllum; Pennisetum clandestinum as Cenchrus clandestinus; Pennisetum macrourum as Cenchrus caudatus; Pennisetum pedicellatum as Cenchrus pedicellatus; Polygonum perfoliatum as Persicaria perfoliata; Prosopis alpataco as Neltuma alpataco; Prosopis argentina as Neltuma argentina; Salsola vermiculata as Caroxylon vermiculatum; Salvinia herzogii as Salvinia biloba. Euphorbia prunifolia is a heterotypic synonym of Euphorbia heterophylla in Kew's checklist, and is matched as that species. Matched only as printed (Kew gives no one accepted species for them, or a broader one): Avena ludoviciana, Pennisetum polystachion, Setaria pallide-fusca.

jurisdictions.edition: Official Compilation of Codes, Rules and Regulations of the State of New York, Title 6, as shown on the Department of State's Westlaw site: Part 575 current through November 15, 2024 (effective March 10, 2015); section 192.1 current through February 28, 2022

classes.prohibited: Prohibited invasive species in New York: no one may sell, import, purchase, transport, introduce or propagate it, or knowingly possess it with the intent to sell, import, purchase, transport or introduce it, except under a Department of Environmental Conservation permit for research, education or other approved activity (6 NYCRR 575.3(b), (c); 575.9(a))
classes.regulated: Regulated invasive species in New York: it may be possessed, sold, bought, propagated and transported, but no one may introduce it into a free-living state (public lands and waters, lands and waters connected to them, natural areas) knowingly or by a means they knew or should have known would lead there, without a permit, and it must be sold, or supplied by a landscaper, with the warning "Invasive Species-Harmful to the Environment" (6 NYCRR 575.4(b), 575.6, 575.9(b))
classes.blackCurrant: Cultivated black currant in New York: planting, growing, propagating, cultivating or selling its plants, roots or cuttings is prohibited, except cultivars immune or resistant to white pine blister rust and except in designated fruiting currant districts (6 NYCRR 192.1)
classes.prohibitedBarberry: Prohibited invasive species in New York: no one may sell, import, purchase, transport, introduce or propagate it, or knowingly possess it with the intent to sell, import, purchase, transport or introduce it, except under a Department of Environmental Conservation permit for research, education or other approved activity; the Department has exempted five cultivars: 'Aurea', Crimson Cutie, Lemon Cutie, Lemon Glow and Mr. Green Genes (6 NYCRR 575.3(b), (c); 575.8; Environmental Notice Bulletin, November 16, 2022)

jurisdictions.notes: Read from the rule's sections as Jason saved them from the Department of State's NYCRR on govt.westlaw.com on 2026-10-31: 575.1 to 575.6 and 575.8 to 575.11, and 192.1. The pages are headed "OFFICIAL COMPILATION OF CODES, RULES AND REGULATIONS OF THE STATE OF NEW YORK", in a window titled "Unofficial New York Codes, Rules and Regulations". Part 575 is "Current through November 15, 2024" and 192.1 "Current through February 28, 2022". The pages print no history notes. The Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) gives Part 575's effective date as March 10, 2015. Not saved: 575.7 (petitions to add or remove species) and 575.12 (severability). Phase-in, past: 575.3(f) let Japanese barberry be possessed, sold, purchased, transported or introduced "for a maximum of one year following the effective date of this Part"; DEC dates the end March 9, 2016. Prohibited plants "shall only be disposed of in a manner that renders them nonliving and nonviable" (575.3(e)). Permits: a prohibited species may be possessed with intent to sell, import, purchase, transport or introduce it under a DEC permit "for research, education, or other approved activity" (575.9(a)). A regulated species may be introduced into a free-living state only under a permit "expressly authorizing such introduction" (575.9(b)). Exemptions, 575.8(a). The Part does not apply to: (1) incidental or unknowing possession, sale and the like, not due to a failure to take reasonable precautions; (2) possession or transport to control or manage an existing infestation; (3) possession or transport for identification or disposal; (4) a cultivar of a listed species that DEC determines reproduces mainly sexually and does not revert to its parent's invasive traits. Such a cultivar must be completely sterile or have no reproductive parts, or demographic modeling must predict it can't establish expanding populations in natural areas. "the department will publish a list of cultivars meeting the criteria of this subparagraph in the State Register and Environmental Notice Bulletin. Only cultivars listed pursuant to this section are eligible for this exemption". The rule itself names no cultivar. DEC's Environmental Notice Bulletin of November 16, 2022 lists nine as "Conditionally Exempt": Berberis thunbergii 'Aurea', 'UCONNBTCP4N' (Crimson Cutie), 'UCONNBTB113' (Lemon Cutie), 'UCONNBTB048' (Lemon Glow) and 'UCONNBTB039' (Mr. Green Genes); Miscanthus sinensis 'NCMS1' (My Fair Maiden) and 'Tift M77' (Scout); Euonymus fortunei 'Kewensis' and 'Vanilla Frosting'. Entries can't except cultivars, so the species are recorded whole, and Japanese barberry's line (prohibitedBarberry) names its five, as Pennsylvania's does; (5) holders of a DEC or Agriculture and Markets permit for disposal, control, research or education; (6) work under a compliance agreement, limited permit or certificate of inspection; (7) permitted biological control agents; (8) wetland plants in a wastewater vegetation treatment unit permitted before the Part was adopted. Regulated species: they "shall be legal to possess, sell, buy, propagate and transport" (575.4(b)). The duties are in 575.6. A sale label or written notice, "Invasive Species-Harmful to the Environment" in at least 14-point bold type, must offer non-invasive alternatives and care instructions. A landscaper must give the customer written notice before supplying or planting one. Buyers must follow and keep the instructions. A free-living state is defined in 575.2(m). It means public lands and waters, lands and waters connected to them, natural areas, and water-using facilities whose outflows give direct access to public waters. For fish and aquatic plants it excludes artificial ponds with no outlet to public waters and private waters not connected to public waters. Agriculture and Markets inspects registered growers and dealers for compliance (575.11). Printed as whole species, and entered so: Phragmites australis (lv), with no exception for the native subspecies; Oplismenus hirtellus (lii), the species, not subspecies undulatifolius; Myriophyllum heterophyllum (xlviii), the species itself, besides the hybrid (xlix). Misspelled: "Hydrocharis morus-ranae" (xxx), entered as printed with Kew's spelling. Left out: (xlix) "Myriophyllum heterophyllum x M. laxum", a hybrid printed by its parents. Printed with synonyms in parentheses, recorded by the first name: Centaurea stoebe (C. biebersteinii, C. diffusa, C. maculosa misapplied, C. xpsammogena), so diffuse knapweed, C. diffusa, appears only as a synonym and is not entered; Cirsium arvense (C. setosum, C. incanum, Serratula arvensis); Cynanchum louiseae (C. nigrum, Vincetoxicum nigrum); Cynanchum rossicum (C. medium, Vincetoxicum medium, V. rossicum); Dioscorea polystachya (D. batatas); Ficaria verna (Ranunculus ficaria); Frangula alnus (Rhamnus frangula); Imperata cylindrica (I. arundinacea, Lagurus cylindricus); Ludwigia hexapetala (L. grandiflora); Persicaria perfoliata (Polygonum perfoliatum); Reynoutria japonica (Fallopia japonica, Polygonum cuspidatum); Reynoutria sachalinensis (Fallopia sachalinensis, Polygonum sachalinensis); "Reynoutria x bohemica (Fallopia x bohemica, Polygonum x bohemica)". "Lonicera x bella" and "Reynoutria x bohemica" are entered with the × sign. Black currant, 6 NYCRR 192.1 (https://govt.westlaw.com/nycrr/Document/I21ef9955c22211ddb7c8fb397c5bd26b): the ban holds statewide, except for cultivars "immune or resistant to white pine blister rust disease or currant rust (Cronartium ribicola) as described in section 192.2" and "in designated fruiting currant districts as defined in section 192.3". 192.2 and 192.3 were not saved, so the resistant cultivars and the districts are not named here. Left out: 192.4, white pine blister rust quarantine districts, which in an unofficial copy bars every Ribes from named counties and towns only; it was not saved, and covers named districts only. Also left out: seed-law lists and advisory lists. Kew's accepted names (2026-10-31), by which these are also matched: Achyranthes japonica as Achyranthes bidentata; Cynanchum louiseae as Vincetoxicum nigrum; Cynanchum rossicum as Vincetoxicum rossicum; Egeria densa as Elodea densa; Ficaria verna as Ranunculus ficaria; Humulus japonicus as Humulus scandens. Matched only as printed (Kew gives no one accepted species for them, or a broader one): Ampelopsis brevipedunculata.
